blocks.text: Quick verdict

Proxy-Cheap is the cheaper pick at almost every volume while its promotion runs: about $7.80 for 10 GB against $35 at Rayobyte, and it supports SOCKS5 and UDP. Rayobyte is the better choice when you need city-level targeting on rotating residential, a US-based vendor with well-regarded human support, or stability in pricing that does not depend on a promotion; its $0.90/GB terabyte rate is also close to Proxy-Cheap's. Test both on your targets, since success rates matter more than a few cents.

Rayobyte and Proxy-Cheap both appeal to buyers who want residential IPs without enterprise prices, and both also sell datacenter and ISP proxies. Proxy-Cheap currently leads at small volumes with a promotional $0.78/GB pay-as-you-go rate. Rayobyte starts higher but falls to $0.90/GB at a terabyte, offers city targeting, and its traffic never expires. Proxy-Cheap supports SOCKS5 and UDP, which Rayobyte's residential gateway does not. This comparison shows which budget option fits your workload.

blocks.text: Rayobyte in 2026: what you get

Rayobyte combines one of the strongest datacenter proxy catalogs with a simple residential offer. Residential traffic is bought in volume bands, from $3.50/GB below 50 GB down to $0.90/GB at a terabyte, and it never expires. Users often praise its human support team. The trade-offs are HTTP-only residential access and limited public data on pool size.

Strengths: Non-expiring residential traffic; Steep volume discounts down to $0.90/GB; Excellent datacenter and ISP catalog; Well-regarded human support. Weak spots: No SOCKS5 or UDP on residential; Pool size not prominently published; Fewer advanced targeting options than enterprise providers.
Proxy-Cheap in 2026: what you get

Proxy-Cheap lives up to its name: rotating residential traffic is currently advertised at $0.78/GB (70% off a $2.60 list price) with no subscription, and static ISP and datacenter IPs cost a dollar or two per month. The catalog is broad, covering IPv6 options few competitors offer, and payment by card, PayPal, Alipay or crypto is easy. The trade-offs are thinner targeting (country and ISP rather than city on rotating residential) and less published performance data than the bigger brands.

Strengths: Very low per-GB price while the promotion runs; No monthly commitment on rotating residential; Broad catalog including IPv6 and static mobile; SOCKS5 with UDP support. Weak spots: Targeting is mostly country and ISP, not city; Residential pool size not separately published; Mixed results in some independent benchmarks.
Pricing: Rayobyte vs Proxy-Cheap
Rayobyte prices residential traffic in four pay-as-you-go bands: $3.50/GB for 1-49 GB, $2/GB for 50-249 GB, $1.50/GB for 250-999 GB and $0.90/GB for 1-5 TB. Traffic does not expire.

Proxy-Cheap's rotating residential proxies are pay-as-you-go, currently listed from $0.78/GB (a promotional price against a $2.60/GB list rate). Static residential ISP proxies start around $2.44 per IP per month, datacenter IPv4 at about $1.49, datacenter IPv6 from $0.15, and rotating mobile at $5.99/GB.

At 10 GB a month, Proxy-Cheap is the cheaper option at about $7.80 against $35 for Rayobyte, roughly 78% less. At 100 GB a month, Proxy-Cheap is the cheaper option at about $78 against $200 for Rayobyte, roughly 61% less. The sticker price is only half of it. Rayobyte's unused traffic carries forward, while Proxy-Cheap's does not (pay-as-you-go balance, no monthly commitment), so if your usage swings from month to month Rayobyte can work out cheaper than the per-GB numbers suggest.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

Rayobyte and Proxy-Cheap do not publish a clear residential pool figure, so a size comparison is not possible on published data. Rayobyte lists 'Not prominently published' and Proxy-Cheap lists 'Not separately published (155M+ claimed across all products)'. In practice, what matters is how many unique IPs you get in the countries you target, which you can measure in a short trial by sending a few thousand requests and counting distinct exit addresses. For coverage, Rayobyte lists Global countries and Proxy-Cheap lists 180+. On targeting, Rayobyte offers country, region and city, while Proxy-Cheap offers country and ISP.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Protocol support is a real difference here. Proxy-Cheap supports HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS5 (TCP and UDP), while Rayobyte offers HTTP, HTTPS (no SOCKS5 on residential). If your tooling needs SOCKS5, for example some anti-detect browsers, desktop apps or non-HTTP traffic, that settles it in Proxy-Cheap's favour. On sessions, Rayobyte offers rotates per request by default; sticky sessions available, and Proxy-Cheap offers rotating and sticky sessions. Both use a backconnect gateway: you point your tool at one host and port, and choose country, city or session behaviour through parameters in the username.
Which is better for your use case?

General web scraping: Rayobyte wins. The deciding factor for Rayobyte: cheap volume bands and traffic that never expires. The limitation on the Proxy-Cheap side: cheap traffic, though independent benchmark results have been mixed.

SERP and rank tracking: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With Rayobyte: usable, with no dedicated SERP product. With Proxy-Cheap: workable for light rank tracking at a low cost. Run the same small test on both before committing.

Social media and multi-account management: Proxy-Cheap. Proxy-Cheap has the edge here. Why: cheap static ISP and mobile IPs for persistent identities. How Rayobyte compares: no SOCKS5 limits some account tools.

E-commerce price and stock monitoring: Rayobyte wins. The deciding factor for Rayobyte: city targeting and low prices at volume. The limitation on the Proxy-Cheap side: fine for country-level price checks.

Ad verification and geo-testing: Rayobyte wins. The deciding factor for Rayobyte: fewer carrier or ASN controls. The limitation on the Proxy-Cheap side: lacks city-level targeting on rotating residential.
Tight budgets: Proxy-Cheap. Proxy-Cheap has the edge here. Why: the lowest advertised per-GB price in this pairing. How Rayobyte compares: $2/GB from 50 GB and $0.90/GB at a terabyte.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. Rayobyte: Check current offer. Proxy-Cheap: 7-day $1.99 trial on static residential and datacenter IPs. Verification and payment rules differ too. Rayobyte: Standard verification; US company. Proxy-Cheap: Light; card, PayPal, Alipay and crypto accepted. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test Rayobyte and Proxy-Cheap before you commit
Spec sheets only get you so far. A short, structured test on your own targets will settle Rayobyte vs Proxy-Cheap faster than any review:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (Rayobyte: check current offer; Proxy-Cheap: 7-day $1.99 trial on static residential and datacenter IPs).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.
3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, Rayobyte comes out ahead in 3, Proxy-Cheap in 2, and 1 is a tie. That makes Rayobyte the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: Rayobyte is strongest for mid-to-high volume scraping on a budget, while Proxy-Cheap is strongest for price-sensitive scraping at moderate difficulty. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
